state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on the misconception that changing all values by the same proportion won't affect the range. Think about how changing all the heights by a certain factor would impact the spread of the data. Can you identify how this change would affect the range of the plant heights?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so if we cut all the plants in half, like divide them all by 2, then the biggest and smallest plants would also get smaller by half... so I guess the difference between them would be smaller too? But I'm still confused about why Katie would be wrong if we just add 3 cm to everything - wouldn't that keep the gap the same?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track in recognizing that changing all values by the same factor will impact the spread of the data. Think about how adding 3 cm to each plant height would affect the range compared to cutting the plants in half. Consider the impact on the differences between the tallest and shortest plants in each scenario.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher explicitly addresses the proportional change misconception and the mathematics is correct, but the scaffolding in Turn 3 doesn't adequately respond to the student's emerging correct understanding about addition, though the student does show clear progress from believing Tom is correct to recognizing both the effect of proportional change and questioning why Katie might be right.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher repeatedly asks the student to 'think about' concepts without breaking the problem into manageable steps or providing scaffolding adjusted to the student's demonstrated confusion, and actually introduces a misconception in Turn 1 by suggesting Tom is correct when he is actually wrong.
